plain_english_title: Date-by-Date Rule Changes for Gulf War Illness, Burn Pit Presumptions & VA Medical Injury Claims
what_this_means: When reviewing older denials involving Gulf War illnesses (38 C.F.R. § 3.317), airborne particulate and PACT Act presumptions (38 C.F.R. §§ 3.320–3.320b), or injuries caused by VA medical care (38 U.S.C. § 1151; 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.358 and 3.361–3.363), the exact year of the claim or decision changes which legal standard applied. For example, diagnosed multisymptom illnesses like fibromyalgia and irritable bowel syndrome were added to § 3.317 effective March 1, 2002; Afghanistan joined § 3.317(a) multisymptom coverage on August 10, 2022; and VA medical injury claims shifted from a 'no-fault' standard to a negligence/unforeseen-event standard for claims received on or after October 1, 1997.
record_clues: A 1995–2002 Gulf War denial rejecting chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, or irritable bowel syndrome because it was a 'diagnosed' illness before Congress expanded 38 U.S.C. § 1117 effective March 1, 2002.
An August 5, 2021 through August 9, 2022 denial of asthma, rhinitis, or sinusitis under 38 C.F.R. § 3.320 because symptoms first appeared more than 10 years after military separation.
A post-2024 claim involving urinary bladder/ureter cancer (§ 3.320a, effective January 2, 2025) or leukemias, multiple myeloma, or myelodysplastic syndromes (§ 3.320b, effective January 10, 2025).

An older 38 U.S.C. § 1151 (or former § 351) VA hospital injury claim filed before October 1, 1997 that may still have remained pending—preserving the pre-1997 no-fault standard under Brown v. Gardner and 38 C.F.R. § 3.358.
important_cautions: Watch Federal Register publication dates versus effective dates: functional gastrointestinal disorder rules published July 15, 2011 (76 FR 41696) took effect August 15, 2011, and VA's post-1997 § 1151 regulations published August 3, 2004 (69 FR 46426) took effect September 2, 2004 (implementing the October 1, 1997 statutory cutoff).

Reopening a finally denied pre-October 1, 1997 § 1151 medical-injury claim on or after October 1, 1997 triggers the modern fault/unforeseen-event standard under 38 C.F.R. § 3.361(a)—so representatives check first whether the pre-1997 claim actually remained pending before filing to reopen.

VA's October 1, 2024 notice updating §§ 3.317 and 3.320 (89 FR 79815) remains a proposed rule that is not finalized, though the PACT Act's statutory text in 38 U.S.C. §§ 1117, 1119, and 1120 is already binding law.

Prospective statutory or regulatory expansions cannot prove Clear and Unmistakable Error (CUE) in final decisions issued before those rules took effect, and 38 C.F.R. § 20.1409(c) permits only one final merits CUE decision per prior Board decision issue.
questions_for_representative: Was my earlier Gulf War or burn-pit denial based on an old geographic, 10-year manifestation, or 10% severity rule that Congress or VA later removed?

If I had a VA medical-injury claim before October 1, 1997, did any unaddressed submission or post-decision medical record under former 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(b) keep that claim pending under the pre-1997 no-fault rule?
How do the effective-date limits in 38 C.F.R. § 3.114(a) compare with submitting newly obtained official service records under 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(c)?
If I am pursuing a PACT Act cancer claim, how do both the statutory presumption in 38 U.S.C. § 1120 and a direct 38 U.S.C. § 1168 TERA nexus opinion work together?
